title: Judge says USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins' religious emails 'go too far'
text:

 BrieAnna J. Frank USA TODAY Nov. 19, 2026 Updated Nov. 20, 2026, 9:06 a.m. ET Hear this story A federal judge on Nov. 19 ordered Department of Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins to "recognize certain boundaries when communicating religious messages" to employees as part of a lawsuit over her alleged Christian proselytizing, saying some of her messages have gone "too far."
 The National Federation of Federal Employees, which represents more than 100,000 federal workers across various agencies, along with several individual USDA employees, sued the department in May. The federal complaint , filed in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, accused Rollins of inappropriate religious messaging, including through an alleged Easter Sunday email to employees that described the holiday as "the greatest story ever told, the foundation of our faith and the abiding hope of all mankind."
 The complaint argued that the alleged emails violate the First Amendment, which bars the government from "respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof," and the Administrative Procedure Act , which governs how federal agencies develop their regulations and procedures.
 U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson’s Nov. 19 order blocked Rollins from taking similar actions while the lawsuit continues. Thompson called Rollins' religious emails "worrisome" and said she has "(portrayed) the agency’s work as a mission to serve her particular Christian views."
 At the same time, Thompson dismissed the plaintiffs' claims related to the Administrative Procedure Act, saying Rollins' messages did not constitute an official agency rule or order.
 Thompson said the court was "keenly aware of the sensitivities present in this action" and that the order "says nothing about the value of prayer or those who believe in its power."
 The boundaries Rollins was ordered to abide by include refraining from such messaging if requested by a colleague, not creating a hostile work environment, or using her authority to pressure subordinates.
 Who gets to watch executions? First Amendment rights are murky Americans United for Separation of Church and State, Democracy Forward and Bryan Schwartz Law are representing the union and federal employees in the case.
 USDA employee Ashley Miller, one of the plaintiffs, said they were "heartened and relieved" by the decision in Americans United's Nov. 19 news release .
 "It was quite scary to come forward, but I am proud that we did so, knowing this will help everyone across USDA," Miller said.
 The union’s president, Randy Erwin , called the ruling an "important victory for the First Amendment," while Americans United president and CEO Rachel Laser said it "should send a message to the Trump administration that it cannot misuse taxpayer resources to preach, hold government-sponsored prayer services during work time, and broadcast Christian Nationalism over official communication channels. Not on our watch."
 In an email to USA TODAY, a USDA spokesperson said the order marked a "completely unprecedented attempt to muzzle a Cabinet secretary" and that the department was "evaluating all options, including a prompt appeal."
